title: Wonder and discovery
hookLine: the Granth's wonder at countless worlds sits easily with curiosity

lines: WORLDS BELOW WORLDS. SKIES ABOVE SKIES.
cards: Worlds below worlds. Skies above skies. That's how one verse of the Japji opens, and it keeps going: people have searched to the very edge and grown tired, and the edge still isn't found.

If the count could be written down, it would be, but the writing runs out first. And the Granth's response to a creation too big to measure isn't fear, or a closed door. It's a word the Gurus come back to with delight.

teach.h: VISMAAD: AWE PAST WHAT THE MIND HOLDS.
teach.b: First, the word. Vismaad: wonder, awe, the astonished stillness when something is bigger than your mind can hold. It isn't confusion.
It's being overwhelmed in the right direction. Second, the Japji's map.

Guru Nanak describes creation as layered past counting, and says plainly it can't be fully written down. That's not a ban on looking. It's an honest note about scale: however far you go, there's farther.
Third, the wonder hymn, which you met early on this path. In Asa di Var the word rings again and again.

teach.h: ASA DI VAR: EVEN KNOWLEDGE IS A WONDER.
teach.b: In paraphrase: wonder the sound, wonder the Vedas, the books of knowledge; wonder the creatures, wonder their kinds; wonder the forms, wonder the colors; wonder the wind, the water, the fire at play; wonder the near, wonder the far.
Look at what sits in that list. The books of knowledge stand right beside the wind and the fire. Learning isn't the end of wonder there.
It's one of the wonders. Fourth, curiosity. Some fear that learning how the world works drains the awe out of it.
The Granth's picture runs the other way: the more you see, the more there is to be astonished by. A Sikh astronomer, or a child with a microscope, isn't trespassing on the sacred.
They're doing vismaad with better instruments.
It turns a page and finds the book is bigger than you thought.

how: Sikhs speak of vismaad as the awe the Gurus describe before creation; the Japji's verse on worlds below and skies above is part of the daily morning prayer.

o: confusion about how the universe first began
a trance in which the mind goes blank and still
awe before a creation too big for the mind to hold

games.q: wonder and discovery: tap the pairs.
p: worlds below worlds, skies above skies
even the books of knowledge are a wonder
runs out before the count does

s: the Granth treats knowledge as the enemy of wonder
in Asa di Var, the books of knowledge are listed among the wonders.
the Japji says creation can be fully written down
if it could be written, it would be; the writing runs out first.
in Asa di Var, Guru Nanak lists wonder after wonder: sound, creatures, colors, wind, water, fire
the word rings again and again, delight before a creation too big to hold.

games.q: a child asks whether learning how stars work will spoil the wonder. what does the Granth's picture suggest?
o: no: the more you see, the more there is to be astonished by.
only learn what scripture already says.
games.why: in Asa di Var, knowledge is one of the wonders; discovery turns a page and the book grows bigger.

practice: Bring to mind one thing about the night sky that's hard to picture: how far, how many, how old. Hold it gently, and on the in-breath let it be large; on the out-breath, notice whether the bigness feels like a threat or a gift.
If you can, let the word come quietly with the out-breath: vismaad.

wordCard.voice: Vismaad. Wonder, awe, the astonished stillness before a creation too big to hold; in Asa di Var, even the books of knowledge are among the wonders. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: vismaad, wonder and awe, the word that rings through Guru Nanak's wonder hymn in Asa di Var.

carryVoice: Your line: wonder keeps learning, not wonder stops learning. Every new fact is one more wonder. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Ang 463–464 (Asa di Var, salok of Guru Nanak: 'vismad naad vismad ved')
